slides.say: n is a positive odd number. The product n, times n plus two, times n plus four, is necessarily divisible by:
So three odd numbers in a row, and what always divides their product. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, the two cases, and then the reason.
at: three odd numbers in a row

slides.say: [short pause] Let's start with the smallest case, one, three and five. One times three times five is fifteen. Forty-five doesn't divide fifteen, so choice number one is out.
But careful, the smallest case only gives a candidate, the biggest number that could work. Fifteen, five and three all divide fifteen, so I need a second case.
Which case? I want to test five, so I choose three odd numbers with no five inside, seven, nine and eleven. Seven times nine is sixty-three, and times eleven is six ninety-three.
It ends in three, so it doesn't divide by five, or by fifteen. Choice numbers two and four are out, and three is left. Choice number three.

Now careful, the trap. Three, five and seven, a hundred five, or five, seven and nine, three fifteen, both divide by fifteen, because each has a five inside. So choose the second case on purpose, avoiding the factor you test.
[pause] And why is three always there? The odd multiples of three are three, nine, fifteen, twenty-one, one in every three odd numbers. So any three odd numbers in a row catch one of them.
Seven, nine, eleven has nine. Eleven, thirteen, fifteen has fifteen. So the product always divides by three. Choice number three. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
